headline: Long-duration illiquid assets such as private equity and venture capital should be held unhedged given prohibitive hedging costs over a 10–15 year horizon.
reasoning: Kelly's view is that for investments with a 10–15 year holding period, such as private equity or venture capital fund commitments, the cost of maintaining a currency hedge over that entire period materially erodes net returns. Over such a long horizon, currency headwinds and tailwinds are expected to balance out, so the terminal currency level at the point of redemption or maturity is what ultimately matters. He therefore takes an entirely unhedged approach to long-duration illiquid positions at Viola Private Wealth.
quote: The way that we approach this is for really long duration investments like private equity or venture capital, where we're looking at taking a position in a fund or an asset over a 10 or 15 year period of time. We have no issue with UN hedged exposures because over that period of time, you know, currency headwinds and tailwinds are going to come and go. What you end up paying is quite a lot of hedging costs over that 10 or 15 year period, which just affects your net return. And really it's at the time that the investment matures or whether the investor chooses to redeem and what the currency is doing at that time that will affect you.
episode_title: Daniel's currency hedging strategy for long-term investors

headline: Income-producing offshore assets including private credit, fixed income and infrastructure should be hedged close to 100% given that currency swings can wipe out annual yield.
reasoning: Kelly argues that for income-generating offshore asset classes — private credit, international fixed income and offshore infrastructure — the proportion of total return delivered as cash income means a 4–5% currency move can almost entirely eliminate the annual yield. He targets a ~100% hedge ratio for these positions and highlights that even funds running at 80–90% hedged have seen meaningful month-to-month performance dispersion from the unhedged residual. Infrastructure is specifically called out because 30–40% of its total return comes from cash-flow payments, making hedging particularly important.
quote: We take a very different approach to income producing funds. So if we're taking international exposure to private credit markets or fixed income, we want to see as close to a 100% hedged ratio on that, because the yields are lower and, you know, a 4 or 5% currency move like we've seen over the last couple of months can almost completely blow up your annual yield. So as the investment trends more towards an income producing asset, we're looking to increase that currency hedging exposure. We've seen even funds that are up at like 80 or 90% hedged. Even that 20% that aren't hedged has been enough to actually throw the month by month performance around, given we've had some pretty wild swings between the Aussie and the US.
episode_title: Daniel's currency hedging strategy for long-term investors

headline: Daniel Kelly outlines currency hedging strategy for long-term endowment-style portfolios, preferring hedged exposure for 5-10 year holdings
reasoning: Kelly notes that the AUD/USD has seen wild swings, with offshore funds recently receiving a 3-4% currency boost as the AUD weakened, but now reverting toward $0.71. He acknowledges he cannot predict where AUD/USD will be in the next 2-5 years, so for long-term endowment-style portfolios he prefers to hold hedged exposure over 5-10 year time horizons. For income-oriented funds, he targets close to a 100% hedge ratio, noting that even an 80-90% hedge ratio leaves enough unhedged exposure to distort month-by-month performance. For risk-averse clients, he recommends hedged share classes to remove currency volatility and deliver a cleaner return profile, though he cautions that currency hedging carries a cost of around 20-30 basis points per annum which compounds materially over a 10-year horizon.
quote: the more proportion that a fund has of income that's coming off it, we want to see as close to a 100% hedge ratio. We've seen even funds that are up at like 80 or 90% hedged. Even that 20% that aren't hedged has been enough to actually throw the month by month performance around, given we've had some pretty wild swings between the Aussie and the US. But look, I don't pretend to know, like I've got the crystal ball and I know, I know where the Aussie US is going to be in the next three or 4 or 5 years, let alone in the next two months. And so when you're building long term endowment style portfolios, you kind of have to think about more than what's happening in the in the current macro environment and think longer term. And so yeah, again, the methodology here is if you're holding an asset for 5 or 10 years, we're happy to take on hedged exposure. There are some clients that are just inherently more risk averse. And so if you've got a client that's risk averse, what is the trend with our advisors to put them into hedged share classes? You just take out the currency volatility. You only receive the underlying asset performance. It makes a bit of a cleaner return profile. You do give up a little bit of total return over the longer term because currency hedging isn't free. It does cost per annum quite often the case 20 or 30 basis points, which might not sound like much, but over a ten year time horizon that starts to add up.
episode_title: Daniel's currency hedging strategy for long-term investors

headline: Currency movements are a 'random walk' in the short term but revert to purchasing power parity over the long term, making hedging strategy an asset-class rather than a market-timing decision.
reasoning: Daniel Kelly argues that short-term currency movements are unpredictable and resemble a random walk, making short-term hedging bets inadvisable. Over the longer term, currencies tend to revert toward purchasing power parity, so the hedging decision should be driven by the nature of the underlying investment rather than a currency forecast. He notes the AUD/USD pair is the dominant consideration for Australian investors given that ~90% of offshore exposures sit in North American markets. The recent move back to ~$0.71 AUD/USD reflects ongoing differential between inflation and interest rate regimes in the two economies.
quote: I always point out to our clients and to our our advisors here that currency movements in the short term are what's called a random walk. So if you're trying to hedge currencies over a 2 or 3 week period, unforeseen economic forces can completely undo that. Generally, currencies hold the purchasing power parity over the longer term. We're not looking at taking any type of currency hedging bet in the short term. We're looking at it from a portfolio construction approach.
episode_title: Daniel's currency hedging strategy for long-term investors

headline: US 30-year Treasury yield volatility and inflation differentials are key drivers of AUD/USD movements and influence Kelly's portfolio hedging decisions.

And so we've seen some pretty big moves in 30 year yields in the US Treasury market, based on what is rolling out there with the buyback program that can affect the interest rate differentials. The inflation regime can kind of affect interest rate differentials. So we're not looking at taking any type of currency hedging bet in the short term.
